cls: Opioid analgesic (weak mu-opioid agonist, methadone congener)
pharm: A centrally acting weak mu-opioid receptor agonist structurally related to methadone; its metabolite norpropoxyphene accumulates and has direct cardiotoxic, local-anesthetic-like effects on cardiac sodium channels prolonging QRS/QT and causing arrhythmia.
quick: Historically 65 mg (HCl) or 100 mg (napsylate) every 4 h as needed (max 390 mg HCl / 600 mg napsylate per day)
May be taken with or without food; with food if GI upset
Avoid; opioid - neonatal dependence/withdrawal with chronic use
Small amounts in milk; generally avoid
Reduce dose / avoid - active metabolite norpropoxyphene accumulates
Reduce dose / avoid - extensive hepatic metabolism, accumulation
Avoid - additive CNS/respiratory depression, fatal in overdose
Withdrawn from US/EU markets for fatal cardiotoxicity and overdose - not recommended
summary: Dextropropoxyphene (propoxyphene) is a weak mu-opioid analgesic, a congener of methadone, that was used for mild to moderate pain, often combined with paracetamol or aspirin. It and especially its long-lived metabolite norpropoxyphene have local-anesthetic, sodium-channel-blocking effects on the heart that prolong the QRS and QT intervals and can cause arrhythmias, conduction block, and cardiac arrest - effects that occur even at therapeutic doses and are not reversed by naloxone. Because of a narrow margin between therapeutic and toxic/fatal doses, high overdose lethality (often combined with alcohol or other CNS depressants), and dose-related cardiac toxicity, dextropropoxyphene was WITHDRAWN from the United States (2010) and the European Union, and is no longer recommended. It is habit forming with opioid dependence and withdrawal potential. This record is provided for historical/safety reference; the drug should not be used.
indications: Relief of mild to moderate pain (historical indication; product withdrawn in US and EU)

dosage.d: 65 mg every 4 hours as needed; maximum 390 mg per day
dosage.n: Historical dosing - product withdrawn; reduce in elderly, renal or hepatic impairment

dosage.d: 100 mg every 4 hours as needed; maximum 600 mg per day
dosage.n: Napsylate 100 mg approximately equivalent to 65 mg hydrochloride; historical only

dosage.d: Use reduced doses and extended intervals, or avoid

admin: NOTE: dextropropoxyphene has been withdrawn from the US and EU markets due to fatal cardiotoxicity - it should not be used
If historically used, take orally with or without food; with food if it upsets the stomach
Do not exceed the maximum daily dose - the gap between effective and toxic doses is narrow
Never combine with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants
Avoid in patients at risk of overdose, suicide, or substance misuse
Naloxone reverses the opioid respiratory depression but NOT the cardiac sodium-channel toxicity
moa: Dextropropoxyphene is a weak agonist at the mu-opioid receptor, producing analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression like other opioids but with relatively low potency. Its principal metabolite, norpropoxyphene, has a long half-life and possesses local-anesthetic (membrane-stabilizing) properties: it blocks cardiac fast sodium channels, slowing conduction (widening QRS), and also affects potassium channels (prolonging QT), which can precipitate bradyarrhythmias, heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, and asystole. This direct cardiotoxicity is dose-related and is the basis for the drug's withdrawal from major markets.

absolute: Use in patients who are suicidal or addiction-prone
Concomitant use with alcohol or other CNS depressants (markedly increases fatal overdose risk)
Marketing withdrawn in US/EU - product no longer available/approved
relative: Pre-existing cardiac conduction abnormalities or QT prolongation
Respiratory disease / risk of respiratory depression
monitor: Signs of opioid dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal
ECG (QRS and QT intervals) where used

preg: Dextropropoxyphene crosses the placenta. Chronic maternal use can cause neonatal opioid dependence and withdrawal, and opioid use late in pregnancy can cause neonatal respiratory depression. There are no adequate well-controlled studies establishing safety; it should be avoided in pregnancy and used, if ever, only when the benefit clearly justifies the risk.
lact: Small amounts of propoxyphene are excreted in breast milk. Because of the potential for sedation and respiratory depression in the nursing infant and the drug's narrow safety margin, breastfeeding should generally be avoided.
renal: Norpropoxyphene, the active and cardiotoxic metabolite, is renally eliminated and accumulates in renal impairment, increasing the risk of cardiac and CNS toxicity. Dose reduction with extended intervals or avoidance is required in renal impairment.
hepatic: Dextropropoxyphene undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism. In hepatic impairment, clearance is reduced and parent drug and metabolite accumulate; dose reduction or avoidance is advised.

major: Alcohol and other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sedatives, other opioids) - additive respiratory and CNS depression; major contributor to fatal overdoses
Carbamazepine - propoxyphene inhibits its metabolism, causing carbamazepine toxicity
Drugs that prolong QT / class I antiarrhythmics - additive cardiac conduction toxicity
moderate: MAO inhibitors - potentiation of opioid effects
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not substantially alter efficacy but reduces GI upset.
interactions.alcohol: Concomitant alcohol markedly increases the risk of severe respiratory/CNS depression and death - strictly avoid. This combination featured in many fatal overdoses.
interactions.diagnostics: May appear as an opioid on urine drug screens; can prolong QRS/QT on ECG.

serious: Cardiac arrhythmias, QRS widening, QT prolongation, conduction block, cardiac arrest (dose-related, from norpropoxyphene)
emergency: Overdose with respiratory depression, coma, cardiac arrhythmia and arrest
Cardiotoxicity (wide QRS, ventricular arrhythmia) - NOT reversed by naloxone

monitoring: Level of consciousness and respiratory rate (opioid effect)
ECG for QRS and QT prolongation where the drug is used
Signs of tolerance, dependence, misuse, and withdrawal
Concomitant CNS depressant and alcohol use
counsel: This medicine has been taken off the market in the US and Europe because of dangerous, sometimes fatal, heart rhythm effects - do not use it
It is an opioid and can be habit forming; never take more than prescribed
Never drink alcohol or take sleeping pills, sedatives, or other opioids with it - the combination can be deadly
It can make you drowsy or dizzy - do not drive or operate machinery
Keep it out of reach of children and others; overdose can be fatal even at modest amounts
If you have been taking it regularly, do not stop suddenly without medical advice to avoid withdrawal
pk: Plasma peak about 2-2.5 hours; norpropoxyphene peaks later
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture (historical product)
pearls: WITHDRAWN in the US (2010, FDA) and EU because of dose-related cardiotoxicity and high overdose lethality - should not be used
Cardiotoxicity (wide QRS, QT prolongation, arrhythmia) is driven by the long-lived metabolite norpropoxyphene and is NOT reversed by naloxone - give sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
Narrow margin between therapeutic and lethal dose; deaths often occurred with alcohol or other CNS depressants and early after ingestion
It is an opioid - habit forming, with dependence, tolerance and withdrawal
Metabolite accumulates in renal and hepatic impairment and in the elderly - higher toxicity risk
Frequently formulated with paracetamol/acetaminophen historically - watch for added hepatotoxicity in overdose
missed: If a dose was missed (historical use), it should be taken when remembered unless it is near the next dose, in which case the missed dose is skipped - never double up. As an opioid that has been withdrawn from major markets, it should not be used; consult a clinician about safer analgesic alternatives.
overdose: Overdose causes opioid effects (respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, stupor progressing to coma) PLUS direct cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, QT prolongation, arrhythmias, bradycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest) and can cause seizures and pulmonary edema; death can occur within the first hour, often with concomitant alcohol. Management: support airway/ventilation, give naloxone for respiratory depression (repeated/infusion doses may be needed but it does NOT reverse cardiotoxicity), treat QRS widening with intravenous sodium bicarbonate, manage arrhythmias and seizures, and provide intensive cardiorespiratory support.
